title: AS Paper 2 mock — Set A: Inflation, trade and policy trade-offs
description: A full 80-mark AS Paper 2 (Theme 2: The UK economy, performance and policies) to be sat in 90 minutes. Section A has four multiple-choice and four short-answer questions on real GDP, aggregate demand, the multiplier, the trade cycle, unemployment measures, investment, the circular flow and output gaps (aim for about 20-25 minutes). Section B is a data response on a fictional small open economy hit by an energy price shock, covering inflation, the current account, SRAS, the exchange rate, monetary policy and conflicts between objectives (about 65 minutes). Show all calculations, use AD/AS diagrams wherever they help, and end every 8+ mark answer with a justified judgement.

questions.prompt: Between two years, a country's nominal GDP rose from £800 billion to £864 billion, while the general price level (measured by the GDP deflator) rose by 5%. What was the approximate rate of growth of real GDP?
questions.explanation: Real GDP = nominal GDP adjusted for inflation. Nominal GDP rose by 8% (864 / 800). Real GDP in the second year at the first year's prices = 864 / 1.05 = about £822.9 billion, an increase of about 2.9% on £800 billion. B is the nominal growth rate, C wrongly adds inflation, and D has the wrong sign.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would cause a movement along an economy's aggregate demand (AD) curve rather than a shift of the curve?
options: A A fall in the general price level
B A cut in Bank Rate
C An increase in government spending on hospitals
D A depreciation of the exchange rate
questions.explanation: The AD curve shows the relationship between the price level and real output demanded, so a change in the price level causes a movement along it (an extension of AD when the price level falls). B, C and D change a component of C + I + G + (X - M) at every price level, so they shift the AD curve.

questions.prompt: In an economy, the marginal propensity to save is 0.1, the marginal propensity to pay tax is 0.2 and the marginal propensity to import is 0.2. If government spending rises by £5 billion, what is the eventual increase in national income?
questions.explanation: The multiplier = 1 / marginal propensity to withdraw = 1 / (0.1 + 0.2 + 0.2) = 1 / 0.5 = 2. The final increase in national income = 2 x £5 billion = £10 billion. D uses 1 / MPS only, ignoring tax and import leakages; A divides instead of multiplying.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is most likely to occur when an economy moves from a boom into a recession?
options: B The government's budget deficit narrows as tax receipts rise
D Spending on imports rises sharply
questions.explanation: In a recession real output falls, so firms need fewer workers and demand-deficient (cyclical) unemployment rises. Inflationary pressure usually eases (A), tax receipts fall and benefit spending rises so the deficit widens (B), and lower incomes reduce spending on imports (D).

questions.prompt: Explain two reasons why the ILO (Labour Force Survey) measure of unemployment and the claimant count may give different figures for the number of people unemployed in the UK.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: ILO measure: people without a job who have actively looked for work in the past four weeks and are available to start within the next two weeks, estimated from the Labour Force Survey. Claimant count: the number of people claiming unemployment-related benefits (Jobseeker's Allowance and Universal Credit claimants required to look for work).
Application/Analysis (any two): Some unemployed people are not eligible to claim (for example because of a partner's income or their savings, or because they are young people or students) or choose not to claim (stigma, complexity), so they appear in the ILO measure but not the claimant count. Some claimants are not unemployed on the ILO definition: under Universal Credit some people in low-paid, part-time work are still required to look for more work and are counted as claimants. The two measures use different methods: one is a sample survey with sampling error, the other is administrative data that changes when benefit rules change.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for a correct definition of the ILO measure; 1 mark for a correct definition of the claimant count; 1 mark for each of two reasons explained (max 2).

questions.prompt: Explain, using the accelerator principle, why investment tends to fluctuate more than consumption over the trade cycle.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Investment is spending on capital goods such as machinery and buildings. The accelerator principle states that the level of net investment depends on the rate of change of national income (or demand), not its level.
Application: A numerical or practical illustration, for example: a firm needs one machine for every £100,000 of sales and replaces one of its ten machines each year; if sales rise by 10%, it needs eleven machines and buys two, so gross investment doubles (a 100% rise) from a 10% rise in demand.
Analysis: Because firms invest to expand capacity in line with expected changes in demand, small changes in the growth of consumption cause proportionately much larger changes in investment. If demand growth merely slows (without falling), net investment falls; if demand falls, firms may stop investing altogether. Swings in business confidence (animal spirits) reinforce this, so investment rises sharply in upturns and collapses in downturns, while consumption is smoothed by habits and savings.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for knowledge of the accelerator (or definition of investment); 1 mark for an application or numerical illustration; up to 2 marks for analysis explaining why changes in the growth of demand cause proportionately larger changes in investment.

questions.prompt: Using the circular flow of income, explain why an increase in household saving may lead to a fall in national income.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: The circular flow of income shows income flowing from firms to households (wages, rent, profit) and back to firms as spending on goods and services. Saving is a withdrawal (leakage) from the circular flow.
Application: If households save a larger proportion of each pound of income (for example because of falling confidence), less is spent on domestically produced goods and services.
Analysis: Firms' revenue falls, so they reduce output and employment, cutting households' incomes; lower incomes lead to further falls in spending (a negative multiplier effect). National income falls until withdrawals again equal injections at a lower equilibrium. Credit a developed point that national income need not fall if banks lend the extra saving to firms for investment (an injection), or reference to the paradox of thrift.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for knowledge of the circular flow or of saving as a withdrawal; 1 mark for application (less spending flowing back to firms); up to 2 marks for analysis (a linked chain through output, employment and incomes, or the multiplier, to a lower equilibrium national income).

questions.prompt: In 2025, an economy's actual real GDP was £2,150 billion and economists estimated its potential real GDP to be £2,200 billion. Calculate the output gap as a percentage of potential GDP, and explain one reason why output gaps are difficult to measure.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: The output gap is the difference between actual real output and potential output (the level consistent with full use of resources without accelerating inflation), usually expressed as a percentage of potential output.
Application: Output gap = (2,150 - 2,200) / 2,200 x 100 = -2.3% (to 1 decimal place), a negative output gap showing spare capacity.
Analysis (one reason, developed): Potential output cannot be observed directly and must be estimated from assumptions about trend productivity growth, the size of the labour force and the natural rate of unemployment; if these change (for example after a shock or a change in migration), estimates are wrong. Data on actual GDP are often revised later, so the gap estimated at the time may change. Different bodies (such as the Office for Budget Responsibility, the Bank of England and the IMF) use different methods and produce different estimates.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for knowledge (definition of output gap); 1 mark for the calculation of -2.3% identified as a negative gap; up to 2 marks for one reason why it is difficult to measure (1 for identification, 1 for development).

questions.prompt: Using Table 1, calculate the overall percentage increase in the price level in Ardenia over 2022 and 2023 combined. Explain what happened to the real value of average earnings over the same two years.
questions.context:
Ardenia: an energy shock and its aftermath (illustrative data)

Table 1: Selected economic indicators for Ardenia, 2021-2025 (illustrative data)
Year | Real GDP growth (%) | CPI inflation (%) | Average earnings growth (%) | Unemployment, ILO (%) | Current account balance (% of GDP) | Policy interest rate, end of year (%) | Exchange rate (crowns per US$, annual average)
2021 | 4.2 | 2.1 | 3.0 | 5.8 | -1.5 | 0.25 | 6.0
2022 | 2.6 | 8.9 | 5.0 | 4.9 | -4.8 | 2.50 | 6.6
2023 | 0.4 | 7.2 | 6.0 | 5.1 | -4.1 | 4.75 | 7.1
2024 | -0.6 | 3.8 | 4.5 | 6.0 | -2.9 | 4.75 | 7.0
2025 | 0.9 | 2.6 | 3.8 | 6.4 | -2.2 | 3.75 | 6.8

Extract A: An imported shock
Ardenia, a fictional small open economy whose currency is the crown, imports around 80% of the gas it uses for heating and electricity generation, and around a third of its food. When world gas prices more than tripled during 2022, household energy bills rose by around 70% and firms in energy-intensive industries such as glass, chemicals and food processing faced sharply higher costs. Because demand for energy is price inelastic in the short run, the value of Ardenia's energy imports rose steeply even though the volume of gas imported fell slightly. The crown also lost value against the US dollar, the currency in which most energy and food is priced. Ardenia's main exports are machinery and financial services; export volumes grew only slowly because its largest trading partners were also hit by the energy shock. Businesses reported that labour shortages, especially in hospitality and logistics, were pushing up wages in 2022 and 2023.

Extract B: The central bank responds
Ardenia's independent central bank has an inflation target of 2%. It raised its policy interest rate from 0.25% at the end of 2021 to 4.75% by the end of 2023, the fastest increase in its history. Around 70% of Ardenian mortgages are fixed for two to five years, so many households only felt the effect of higher rates when their fixed deals ended. House prices fell by around 6% between 2022 and 2024, and business investment fell in both 2023 and 2024. Some economists argued that raising interest rates could do little about inflation caused by world gas prices; the central bank replied that it needed to stop high inflation becoming built into wage settlements and expectations. Inflation fell back towards the target by 2025, but critics blame the bank for the recession of 2024.

Extract C: A fiscal dilemma for 2026
With unemployment rising, the government is considering a fiscal stimulus for 2026 worth around 1.5% of GDP, made up of cuts in income tax and extra spending on road and rail projects. However, the budget deficit is already around 5% of GDP and government debt is around 95% of GDP. The central bank has warned that a large stimulus could push inflation back above target and delay further cuts in interest rates. Business groups support the infrastructure spending but argue that the tax cuts would mainly boost spending on imported consumer goods.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, measured here by the consumer prices index (CPI). Real earnings are nominal earnings adjusted for inflation, showing purchasing power.
Application: Price level: 1.089 x 1.072 = 1.167, an increase of about 16.7% (simple addition giving 16.1% gains only 1 of the 2 calculation marks). Earnings: 1.05 x 1.06 = 1.113, an increase of about 11.3%. Real earnings: 1.113 / 1.167 = 0.953, a fall of about 4.7% (accept around 5%, or year-by-year falls of about 3.6% in 2022 and 1.1% in 2023, approximated as 3.9 and 1.2 percentage points by simple subtraction).
Analysis: Because prices rose faster than earnings in both years, the purchasing power of the average wage fell; households could buy fewer goods and services with their income, reducing living standards and likely restraining consumption. Price increases compound, so the cumulative rise exceeds the sum of the two annual rates.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for knowledge (definition of inflation or real earnings); 2 marks for the price level calculation (1 for compounding method, 1 for 16.7%); 2 marks for real earnings (1 for showing earnings rose less than prices, for example 11.3% versus 16.7%, and 1 for explaining that real earnings fell by around 4.7% so purchasing power fell).

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: The current account records trade in goods and services, primary income and secondary income; a deficit means outflows exceed inflows.
Application/Analysis (any two, using the data): Higher energy import bill: world gas prices more than tripled and demand for gas is price inelastic, so spending on imports rose steeply even though the volume of imports fell slightly; the deficit widened from 1.5% to 4.8% of GDP. Depreciation of the crown (6.0 to 6.6 crowns per US$): imports priced in dollars, including energy and food, became about 10% more expensive in crowns; with inelastic demand in the short run, import spending rose (J-curve effect). Weak export growth: Ardenia's main trading partners were also hit by the energy shock, so demand for its machinery and financial services exports grew slowly. Strong domestic demand: real GDP still grew 2.6% and unemployment fell to 4.9%, raising incomes and spending on imports.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for knowledge of the current account or a current account deficit; for each of two reasons, 1 mark for identification and 1 mark for explanation using Extract A or Table 1 (max 4).

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) shifts left when firms' costs of production rise, for example raw materials and energy; cost-push inflation; stagflation (rising prices with falling or slowing output); AD/AS diagram.
Application: World gas prices more than tripled; 80% of gas imported; energy bills up around 70%; energy-intensive industries (glass, chemicals, food processing); depreciation raised dollar-priced import costs; CPI inflation 8.9% in 2022 and 7.2% in 2023; real GDP growth slowed from 4.2% to 2.6% and then 0.4%.
Analysis: Higher energy costs raise firms' costs at every level of output, so SRAS shifts left from SRAS1 to SRAS2; at the original price level there is excess demand, so the price level rises from P1 to P2 and real output falls from Y1 to Y2 (or grows more slowly), giving cost-push inflation and stagflation. Further chains: higher energy bills cut households' real incomes (real earnings fell), reducing consumption and shifting AD left, which offsets some of the price rise but deepens the fall in output; wage rises from labour shortages add a second round of cost-push.
Evaluation: The size of the effects depends on the share of energy in costs: energy-intensive sectors are hit hard, services less so. Not all of the slowdown was caused by gas prices: rising interest rates (0.25% to 4.75%) and weak trading partners also reduced AD. The shock may be temporary; as gas prices fall SRAS shifts back, which helps explain inflation falling to 2.6% by 2025. Government support for energy bills could limit the effect. Judgement on how much of 2022-23's stagflation the gas shock explains.
Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis (KAA) up to 5 marks; Evaluation up to 3 marks.
Levels:
KAA Level 1 (1-2 marks): Isolated or partially accurate knowledge; little or no application to the context or data; analysis is absent or consists of unconnected assertions.
KAA Level 2 (3-4 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some use of the data; chains of reasoning are developed but may be incomplete or one-sided, and diagrams may contain minor errors or not be explained.
KAA Level 3 (5 marks): Precise, relevant knowledge applied consistently to the context, using the data selectively; analysis develops clear, logical, multi-step chains of reasoning, supported by accurate diagrams integrated into the answer where relevant.
Evaluation Level 1 (1-2 marks): Evaluative comments are generic, asserted or unsupported by evidence; no clear judgement.
Evaluation Level 2 (3 marks): Relevant evaluation that is supported by evidence from the extracts or wider knowledge, weighing arguments and reaching a reasoned judgement.
A* answer: Draws an accurate AD/AS diagram showing SRAS shifting left with the new price level and output labelled, uses Table 1 figures to show stagflation, adds a second chain on the AD effects of falling real incomes, and evaluates by separating the gas shock from other causes such as interest rates and judging its relative importance.

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Exchange rate and net trade: a depreciation makes exports cheaper in foreign currency and imports more expensive in domestic currency; net trade (X - M) is a component of AD; price elasticity of demand for exports and imports; the J-curve; the Marshall-Lerner condition may be credited.
Application: Crowns per US$ rose from 6.0 to 7.1, so the crown's value fell from about $0.167 to about $0.141, a depreciation of roughly 15%; energy and food priced in dollars; energy demand price inelastic; exports of machinery and financial services; trading partners hit by the energy shock; current account deficit 4.8% (2022) and 4.1% (2023) of GDP.
Analysis: Exports: Ardenian machinery and financial services become cheaper for foreign buyers, so export volumes and revenues should rise, increasing (X - M) and shifting AD right, with multiplier effects on output and employment. Imports: imports become more expensive in crowns; if demand is price elastic, import spending falls, raising net trade further. But because most imports are energy and food with inelastic demand, import spending in crowns rises, so net trade may worsen at first (J-curve) and AD may shift left. Higher import prices also reduce households' real incomes and consumption, and raise firms' costs (SRAS shifts left), adding to inflation.
Evaluation: The overall effect on AD depends on the price elasticities of exports and imports; with inelastic energy imports and weak demand in trading partners, the short-run effect is probably small or negative, and the current account only improved from 2023 onwards. Non-price competitiveness (quality of machinery) may matter more than price. Time lags: contracts are fixed in advance, so volumes adjust slowly. Other factors were changing at the same time (interest rates rising, world gas prices), so the effect of the depreciation cannot be isolated. Judgement.

Levels:
KAA Level 1 (1-2 marks): Isolated or partially accurate knowledge; little or no application to the context or data; analysis is absent or consists of unconnected assertions.
KAA Level 2 (3-4 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some use of the data; chains of reasoning are developed but may be incomplete or one-sided, and diagrams may contain minor errors or not be explained.
KAA Level 3 (5-6 marks): Precise, relevant knowledge applied consistently to the context, using the data selectively; analysis develops clear, logical, multi-step chains of reasoning, supported by accurate diagrams integrated into the answer where relevant.
Evaluation Level 1 (1-2 marks): Evaluative comments are generic, asserted or unsupported by evidence; no clear judgement.
Evaluation Level 2 (3-4 marks): Relevant evaluation that is supported by evidence from the extracts or wider knowledge, weighing arguments and reaching a reasoned judgement.
A* answer: Calculates the depreciation accurately from Table 1, analyses separate chains for exports, imports and real incomes, explains why inelastic energy imports and weak trading partners could make the effect on AD small or even negative (J-curve), and reaches a supported judgement using the trend in the current account.

Knowledge: Monetary policy and the transmission mechanism: higher interest rates raise the cost of borrowing and the reward for saving, increase mortgage payments, reduce asset prices and wealth, may raise the exchange rate, and dampen inflation expectations; AD shifts left, reducing demand-pull inflation. Distinction between demand-pull and cost-push inflation.
Application: Rate rose from 0.25% to 4.75%; CPI inflation fell from 8.9% (2022) to 2.6% (2025); 70% of mortgages fixed for two to five years; house prices fell around 6%; business investment fell in 2023 and 2024; earnings growth peaked at 6.0% in 2023 and fell to 3.8%; real GDP fell 0.6% in 2024; unemployment rose from 4.9% to 6.4%.
Analysis: Higher rates reduce consumption (higher mortgage costs as fixed deals end, more saving, negative wealth effect from falling house prices) and investment (higher cost of borrowing, lower confidence), shifting AD left and reducing demand-pull pressure, including in the labour market, which slows wage growth. Firmly anchored expectations prevent a wage-price spiral, so second-round effects of the gas shock are limited. Diagram: AD shifting left, lowering the price level (or its rate of increase) and real output.
Evaluation: Inflation was mainly imported cost-push from gas and food; interest rates cannot lower world energy prices, so much of the fall in inflation probably reflects gas prices falling back rather than policy. Time lags: with 70% of mortgages fixed, much of the effect arrived in 2024, after inflation had already started to fall. The crown continued to weaken until 2023, so the exchange-rate channel was weak. Costs: recession in 2024 and rising unemployment suggest the policy was effective in reducing demand but at a high price. However, falling earnings growth after 2023 suggests the policy prevented inflation becoming embedded. Judgement: partially effective, mainly through expectations and the labour market.
Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis (KAA) up to 8 marks; Evaluation up to 4 marks.
Levels:
KAA Level 1 (1-2 marks): Isolated or partially accurate knowledge; little or no application to the context or data; analysis is absent or consists of unconnected assertions.
KAA Level 2 (3-5 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some use of the data; chains of reasoning are developed but may be incomplete or one-sided, and diagrams may contain minor errors or not be explained.
KAA Level 3 (6-8 marks): Precise, relevant knowledge applied consistently to the context, using the data selectively; analysis develops clear, logical, multi-step chains of reasoning, supported by accurate diagrams integrated into the answer where relevant.
Evaluation Level 1 (1-2 marks): Evaluative comments are generic, asserted or unsupported by evidence; no clear judgement.
Evaluation Level 2 (3-4 marks): Relevant evaluation that is supported by evidence from the extracts or wider knowledge, weighing arguments and reaching a reasoned judgement.
A* answer: Explains several transmission channels in linked chains with an AD/AS diagram, uses the data on rates, inflation, house prices, investment and earnings, and evaluates by distinguishing cost-push from demand-pull inflation, considering time lags from fixed-rate mortgages and the cost of recession, reaching a balanced judgement on how much of the fall in inflation the rate rises caused.

questions.prompt: Evaluate whether the government of Ardenia should introduce the proposed fiscal stimulus in 2026, given the possible conflicts between its macroeconomic objectives.
questions.context:
Ardenia: an energy shock and its aftermath (illustrative data)

Table 1: Selected economic indicators for Ardenia, 2021-2025 (illustrative data)
Year | Real GDP growth (%) | CPI inflation (%) | Average earnings growth (%) | Unemployment, ILO (%) | Current account balance (% of GDP) | Policy interest rate, end of year (%) | Exchange rate (crowns per US$, annual average)
2021 | 4.2 | 2.1 | 3.0 | 5.8 | -1.5 | 0.25 | 6.0
2022 | 2.6 | 8.9 | 5.0 | 4.9 | -4.8 | 2.50 | 6.6
2023 | 0.4 | 7.2 | 6.0 | 5.1 | -4.1 | 4.75 | 7.1
2024 | -0.6 | 3.8 | 4.5 | 6.0 | -2.9 | 4.75 | 7.0
2025 | 0.9 | 2.6 | 3.8 | 6.4 | -2.2 | 3.75 | 6.8

Extract A: An imported shock
Ardenia, a fictional small open economy whose currency is the crown, imports around 80% of the gas it uses for heating and electricity generation, and around a third of its food. When world gas prices more than tripled during 2022, household energy bills rose by around 70% and firms in energy-intensive industries such as glass, chemicals and food processing faced sharply higher costs. Because demand for energy is price inelastic in the short run, the value of Ardenia's energy imports rose steeply even though the volume of gas imported fell slightly. The crown also lost value against the US dollar, the currency in which most energy and food is priced. Ardenia's main exports are machinery and financial services; export volumes grew only slowly because its largest trading partners were also hit by the energy shock. Businesses reported that labour shortages, especially in hospitality and logistics, were pushing up wages in 2022 and 2023.

Extract B: The central bank responds
Ardenia's independent central bank has an inflation target of 2%. It raised its policy interest rate from 0.25% at the end of 2021 to 4.75% by the end of 2023, the fastest increase in its history. Around 70% of Ardenian mortgages are fixed for two to five years, so many households only felt the effect of higher rates when their fixed deals ended. House prices fell by around 6% between 2022 and 2024, and business investment fell in both 2023 and 2024. Some economists argued that raising interest rates could do little about inflation caused by world gas prices; the central bank replied that it needed to stop high inflation becoming built into wage settlements and expectations. Inflation fell back towards the target by 2025, but critics blame the bank for the recession of 2024.

Extract C: A fiscal dilemma for 2026
With unemployment rising, the government is considering a fiscal stimulus for 2026 worth around 1.5% of GDP, made up of cuts in income tax and extra spending on road and rail projects. However, the budget deficit is already around 5% of GDP and government debt is around 95% of GDP. The central bank has warned that a large stimulus could push inflation back above target and delay further cuts in interest rates. Business groups support the infrastructure spending but argue that the tax cuts would mainly boost spending on imported consumer goods.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Expansionary fiscal policy (tax cuts and higher government spending) shifts AD right; the multiplier; macroeconomic objectives (growth, low unemployment, low and stable inflation, current account balance, balanced budget/sustainable debt); trade-offs such as the short-run Phillips curve relationship between inflation and unemployment; interaction with monetary policy; supply-side effects of infrastructure.
Application: Stimulus of around 1.5% of GDP; unemployment up from 4.9% to 6.4% and growth weak (0.9% in 2025), suggesting a negative output gap; inflation 2.6%, close to the 2% target; budget deficit around 5% of GDP and debt around 95% of GDP; current account deficit 2.2% of GDP; central bank warning about delaying rate cuts; business view that tax cuts mainly boost imports.
Analysis: Benefits: higher AD raises real output and reduces cyclical unemployment through the multiplier; infrastructure spending also raises LRAS in the long run (better transport), increasing potential growth and reducing inflationary pressure later. Conflicts: with inflation only just above target, higher AD may raise demand-pull inflation (Phillips curve trade-off); tax cuts increase spending on imports, worsening the current account; higher borrowing widens the deficit and increases debt, which may raise interest costs and require future tax rises or spending cuts; the central bank may keep rates higher, crowding out private investment and offsetting the stimulus.
Evaluation: Depends on the size of the output gap: unemployment of 6.4% versus 4.9% in 2022 suggests spare capacity, so inflationary risk may be modest. The multiplier is likely small in a very open economy with a high propensity to import, especially for tax cuts; infrastructure spending has a larger multiplier and supply-side benefits but long time lags. Debt at around 95% of GDP limits fiscal space, but borrowing for investment may be justified if it raises future growth. Coordination with the central bank matters: a smaller, investment-focused stimulus may allow rate cuts to continue. Prioritised judgement, for example: favour the infrastructure element but scale back the tax cuts.
Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis (KAA) up to 12 marks; Evaluation up to 8 marks.
Levels:
KAA Level 1 (1-3 marks): Isolated knowledge, often limited to definitions; little or no application to the context; analysis is descriptive or confused.
KAA Level 2 (4-6 marks): Mostly accurate knowledge with some application to the context and data; chains of reasoning are partial or not clearly linked to the question; diagrams, if used, contain errors or are not explained.
KAA Level 3 (7-9 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with relevant use of data from the extracts; several developed chains of reasoning, though some lack depth or balance; diagrams are mostly accurate and referred to.
KAA Level 4 (10-12 marks): Precise, wide-ranging knowledge applied throughout, integrating data from the extracts; fully developed, coherent chains of reasoning covering both sides of the issue; accurate diagrams are integrated into the argument.
Evaluation Level 1 (1-3 marks): Evaluative comments are generic or asserted, with little reference to the context; no supported judgement.
Evaluation Level 2 (4-6 marks): Evaluation addresses relevant issues with some support from the extracts, but is not fully developed, not prioritised or lacks a clear final judgement.
Evaluation Level 3 (7-8 marks): Sustained, well-supported evaluation that weighs the arguments, prioritises the most significant factors, recognises what the answer depends on and reaches a fully justified judgement.
A* answer: Analyses the stimulus against each macroeconomic objective using Table 1 and Extracts B and C, explains the main trade-offs (inflation versus unemployment, external balance, fiscal sustainability, interaction with monetary policy) with AD/AS reasoning, distinguishes between the tax-cut and infrastructure elements, and reaches a clear, conditional judgement on whether and in what form the stimulus should go ahead.
